image-alt: "Diff-in-diff chart of Google search interest in The Beatles around the Now and Then release, compared to control bands"
description: "A diff-in-diff test of how the 2023 Now and Then release lifted search interest in the Beatles' entire catalogue, not just the new song."
---

In 2023 the Beatles released a new song. The interesting question is not how it charted. It is what it did to searches for everything else they ever recorded.

"Now and Then" came out on 2 November 2023, billed as the last new Beatles track, built from a decades-old Lennon demo. I pulled Google Trends for "The Beatles" against three legacy bands with no shock in the window (Stones, Zeppelin, Pink Floyd) and ran the same diff-in-diff from my Get Back post.

First surprise: attention started moving a full week before there was anything to hear. The teaser and the announcement, with not a note of music released yet, lifted searches about 30% off baseline. The peak week bundles the short film and the release itself, so the cleanest evidence that promotion moves people is that pre-release jump, before the product existed publicly.

Second surprise: the effect after release was roughly half of Get Back's. But it did not fully fade. Three months out, Beatles search interest was still above where the pre-launch trend put it, while the control bands sat flat. A new song, even one built from an old cassette, left a longer afterglow on the whole catalogue than an 8-hour documentary did.

Product launches work the same way. An iPhone announcement starts moving people well before launch day, and the halo on the rest of the product line often outlasts both.

What lifts your back catalogue more, the trailer or the thing itself?
